Planning for two lives: show one-survivor years beside the household budget

Read Canadian period-life-table observations, test a joint-survival assumption and build a separate two-phase retirement funding schedule with four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep the joint-life illustration separate from a household budget scenario

The central idea

A household plan needs room for the years with two people and the years with one survivor. Keep population statistics, dependence assumptions and spending scenarios distinct.

01

Compare survival from a common starting age

For a household beginning retirement with two people, the plan may need to continue while either is alive. Looking at one person’s average remaining lifetime does not describe that joint funding period. Start by asking which people are being represented, the age from which survival is measured and the assumption connecting their remaining lifetimes.

The first chart uses a dated Canadian population snapshot: Statistics Canada’s preliminary 2022–2024 three-year period life table, released on 13 January 2026 and retrieved on 25 October 2026. It preserves the source categories Males and Females. Within each category, the displayed share surviving from age 65 to age x is lx ÷ l65.

The starting shares are both 100% because this is conditional on reaching 65. Dividing the later count by the table’s original synthetic cohort of 100,000 would answer a different question. These are period-table calculations using population mortality conditions, not a survey of retired couples or a forecast of an individual’s health.

02

At least one survivor is a different event from both surviving

Consider an illustrative pair, one represented by each source category and both age 65 at the start. Assume, for the example, that the two population marginal survival shares apply to that pair. Let a and b be those shares at a later common age. The event that at least one is alive includes cases where both are alive and cases with exactly one survivor.

If the remaining lifetimes are additionally assumed independent, the chance neither is alive is (1 − a)(1 − b). Subtracting from one gives the at-least-one result: 1 − (1 − a)(1 − b). The both-alive share is ab, while the exactly-one share is a(1 − b) + b(1 − a).

At age 90, the retained source marginal shares are about 29.14% and 42.00%. The independent-pair calculation gives about 58.91% for at least one survivor. That last number is an original assumption-based calculation. It is not an official observation that 58.91% of Canadian couples alive at 65 will have a survivor at 90.

03

Use the bounds to see what independence adds

Marginal survival shares alone do not identify a joint distribution. Keeping a and b fixed, the at-least-one probability can range from max(a,b) to min(1,a + b). The lower endpoint allows the smaller survival event to sit wholly inside the larger one; the upper endpoint allows as little overlap as those marginal shares permit.

For the age-90 values above, that mathematical range is approximately 42.00% to 71.15%, with the independence result between them. The matrix shows the same comparison at several ages. These rows are dependence cases, not optimistic and pessimistic market forecasts, confidence intervals or estimates of statistical sampling error.

Actual couples can also differ from the population marginals because of health, shared circumstances, age differences and selection into the household. The bounds hold the illustrative marginals fixed, so they do not capture every uncertainty about an actual couple. A personal projection needs an appropriate basis; changing only a dependence assumption cannot solve a mismatch in the underlying population.

04

Build the one-survivor cash gap independently

The budget chart is deliberately a separate exercise. It uses one annual portfolio-funded gap while both people are alive and another after a manually selected transition year. The tool does not draw that year from the life table or predict when anyone will die.

The default assumes CAD 24,000 a year for the first fourteen years and CAD 18,000 from year fifteen onward, expressed in today’s dollars. The later gap is 75% of the earlier one because those are the chosen inputs, not because one-person costs follow a standard fraction. The one-survivor gap can also be higher if that is the scenario you need to examine.

Construct each gap after separately reviewing spending and the income available in that household state. Some bills may continue while income sources change; benefit entitlement, taxes and payment timing require their own checks. This tool does not calculate those changes or infer them from the number of people remaining.

05

Discount the selected schedule without hiding a mortality assumption

For a year-end gap Gt, a constant annual real return r and a horizon N, the displayed present value is the sum of Gt ÷ (1 + r)t for t = 1 to N. The real-dollar convention keeps the gap’s purchasing power basis consistent with the discount rate. No second inflation deduction is applied.

The default thirty-year schedule totals CAD 624,000 before discounting. At the selected 2% real assumption, its present value is about CAD 475,774. Those figures describe the chosen deterministic schedule. They do not survival-weight its payments, price an annuity or establish a guaranteed reserve requirement.

The matrix changes real return and the number of funded years while retaining the two gaps and transition year. A transition beyond a cell’s finish date does not occur in that cell. Compare several horizons and less favourable returns before treating one result as a workable funding plan.

06

Retain the years outside the chart as an explicit open question

The retained life-table extract ends at age 100. Its survival shares are still positive there. The plot therefore stops because the selected data stop; it does not say everyone has died by that age. The article does not calculate a joint life expectancy from this truncated extract.

Likewise, the cash scenario stops at the chosen horizon. It assigns no cost to later years and supplies no automatic income beyond them. A household can plan a longer horizon, consider separately verified dependable income or use other resources, but each extension needs its own cash flows and assumptions.

Use these charts to keep the questions visible: what is observed about the population, what must be assumed to represent a pair, how might the household funding gap change, and which years remain unfunded by the selected schedule? An average, a probability curve and a cash budget each contribute evidence without replacing the others.
